name: Alfalfa (Medicago sativa)
short: Lupus-like illness or flares with alfalfa seed or tablets (case reports; tablet cases called controversial; animal data). Letter title: pancytopenia while taking seeds. Sprouts: Salmonella outbreak.
text: A review of L-canavanine, an amino acid present in alfalfa, states that an association between alfalfa and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) was first reported in a volunteer who developed lupus-like autoimmunity while taking alfalfa seed in a study of high cholesterol, that monkeys fed alfalfa sprouts developed SLE, and that some mouse strains fed L-canavanine showed SLE being triggered or worsened while studies in another strain were negative; the same review calls the induction or worsening of SLE by alfalfa tablets, reported in a few cases, controversial, and says epidemiological studies are sparse. One published letter is titled as reporting exacerbation of SLE associated with alfalfa ingestion and another as reporting pancytopenia (low counts of all blood cell types) during ingestion of alfalfa seeds; neither has an abstract. A review of herbal supplements in autoimmune skin disease notes that in vitro and in vivo studies (the abstract does not name the species studied) have shown alfalfa activating immune cells and that case reports suggest an association between immunostimulatory herbs in general and the onset or flares of lupus, dermatomyositis and autoimmune blistering disorders, and a nutrition review lists L-canavanine in alfalfa tablets among substances that appear to aggravate lupus, while noting that its findings rest on few studies, many uncontrolled or extrapolated from animals. Separately, alfalfa sprouts eaten as food caused a Salmonella outbreak of 31 cases in South Australia in 2018 traced to one producer. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
